post1.text:
Your exit strategy should be built into your growth strategy from day one. Most founders treat them as separate conversations. That mistake costs millions.

Entrepreneur recently highlighted how founders who wait until they are ready to sell to think about their exit consistently leave value on the table. The window to maximize your multiple is not the twelve months before a transaction. It is the three to five years before that.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M need to understand:

First, buyers do not pay for revenue. They pay for predictable, recurring, transferable revenue. Those are three very different things.

Second, your EBITDA margin matters less than your EBITDA trend. A business growing margin year over year commands a premium that a static business simply cannot match.

Third, leadership dependency is a valuation killer. If the business cannot run without you, acquirers will price that risk into their offer.

You are building something valuable. The question is: are you building it in a way that someone else will pay full price to own?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank lays out the core business exit strategies available to owners, from strategic sales to private equity recaps to family succession. It is a solid overview. But here is what it does not tell you: the strategy you choose at exit is largely determined by decisions you made years earlier.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this distinction is critical. The operational infrastructure you build, the customer concentration you allow, the management bench you develop or neglect, all of it shapes which exit paths are even available to you.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who want every option on the table when the time comes. That requires intentional planning long before any banker calls.

Read the J.P. Morgan piece, then ask yourself honestly: which of these paths are you actually positioned for right now?

post3.text:
Silicon Valley Bank recently published a breakdown of when founders should and should not sell. The timing question is real. But timing is only one variable. The bigger question is whether your business is built to command the multiple you deserve when that moment arrives.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles exactly this. Titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit and authored by Paul Belair and George Hohman, the chapter gives scaling companies a concrete lens for understanding what sophisticated buyers actually look for during due diligence.

One thing Paul and George make clear: the gap between what founders think their business is worth and what the market will pay is almost always explained by factors inside the owner's control. That is both the challenge and the opportunity.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because leadership teams treat execution as an afterthought.

Forbes recently broke down the core reasons leadership teams collapse at strategy execution. The pattern is consistent: leaders confuse planning with doing, and they mistake activity for progress.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

1. They build plans for the board, not for the people running the business day to day. A strategy no one can act on is just a document.

2. They skip the ownership conversation. Every priority needs a name attached to it. Not a department. A person.

3. They review strategy annually but run the business weekly. That gap is where growth stalls.

If your company is between $50M and $500M, the strategic planning process that got you here will not get you there. The mechanics have to change.

So here is the question worth sitting with: Does your leadership team know the three most important things to accomplish this quarter, and can they say them without looking at a slide?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes laid out exactly why leadership teams break down when it comes to strategy execution, and the findings should concern any CEO running a company between $50M and $500M.

The core problem is not a lack of smart people or good ideas. It is a structural failure in how strategy gets translated into daily decisions.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with scaling companies. Leadership aligns in the conference room and fragments in the hallway. The plan looks clean on paper and falls apart in execution because no one built the bridge between strategy and operations.

If your team is experiencing that gap, you are not alone and it is fixable. Start by reading the Forbes piece, then ask yourself whether your current planning process was built to scale.

post3.text:
Strategy execution looks very different when you are selling fish food versus Nike shoes. That sounds like a strange place to start a conversation about scaling a business, but it is exactly where Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall begin in Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business.

The chapter is titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes" and it draws on real operational experience across wildly different industries to surface one critical insight: the fundamentals of strategic planning do not change, but the way you apply them has to match your business model and your growth stage.

Leaders at companies pushing past $50M often assume their planning process is fine because it worked before. Rafa and Jim challenge that assumption directly and show what a better approach actually looks like in practice.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most leadership teams have a strategy. Very few have a functioning system for executing it. Between $50M and $500M, that gap is not a minor inefficiency. It is the difference between scaling and stalling. The companies that break through are not smarter. They are more deliberate about how strategy connects to the decisions being made on Tuesday morning.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses are completely blind to what that feeling actually is.

Adweek recently profiled creative leaders who successfully transformed legacy brands into cultural touchstones. The common thread was not a bigger ad budget. It was radical honesty about what the brand actually stood for versus what leadership assumed it stood for.

Here is what scaling companies consistently get wrong about marketing:

First, they confuse familiarity with trust. Customers knowing your name does not mean they believe your promise.

Second, they invest in channels before they have clarity on positioning. You cannot amplify a message you have not defined.

Third, they treat brand as a marketing department problem. At the growth stage, brand is a leadership problem.

Ulta's CMO put it plainly: brand building and performance marketing are not competing priorities. They are the same job done at different time horizons.

What does your company's brand actually smell like to someone who has never heard of you?

#Branding #BusinessGrowth #ScalingUp

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive features Ulta's CMO breaking down how she balances brand building with omnichannel performance marketing. It is a genuinely useful read, and it raises something every scaling company needs to confront.

Most businesses in the $50M to $500M range treat brand and demand generation as separate budgets, separate teams, and separate conversations. That split is expensive. When brand and channel strategy are not integrated, you end up paying more to acquire customers who stay less.

The companies that scale with margin intact are the ones where marketing tells a consistent story at every touchpoint, not just in campaigns. That requires alignment between leadership and marketing that most growing companies have not built yet.

Worth reading if you are rethinking how your marketing investments compound over time.

Adweek recently asked four marketing leaders how they turned established brands into cultural icons. The answers had nothing to do with tactics. They had everything to do with knowing what the brand stood for at a level deep enough to guide every decision.

Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, titled What Does Your Marketing Smell Like, tackles this head-on. Written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, the chapter gives leaders at the $50M and beyond stage a framework for diagnosing whether their marketing is actually building the company they are trying to become, or just spending money in the right categories.

One idea from the chapter that stops executives cold: your prospects can smell inconsistency before they can name it. And inconsistency at scale is a growth ceiling.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as ambition.

Most companies scaling past $50M default to headcount as the answer to every operational bottleneck. They hire broadly, onboard slowly, and wonder why the problems persist. SHRM's recent research on 2026 hiring trends confirms what strong operators already know: precision beats volume every time.

Here is what that actually means for leaders at your stage:

First, define the role before you post it. Not the title. The specific outcomes you need in 90 days. If you cannot articulate that, you are not ready to hire.

Second, your top performers are a data source. Study what they do differently and hire backward from that profile, not from a generic job description.

Third, speed of hire and quality of hire are not opposites. A rigorous, focused process closes faster because both sides know exactly what they are evaluating.

Talent strategy at scale is not about filling seats. It is about making every seat count.

Where is your hiring process built around precision, and where is it still built around hope?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Yahoo Finance covered Cognizant's decision to adopt Oracle Fusion Cloud Recruiting to standardize talent acquisition across their global workforce.

For enterprise-scale companies, that headline makes sense. But here is what scaling companies between $50M and $500M need to hear: the lesson is not about the software.

It is about the decision to systematize recruiting before growth exposes every gap in the process.

Companies that wait until hiring feels chaotic to build infrastructure are always playing catch-up. The leaders who scale well treat recruiting as a repeatable business function, not a reactive scramble.

If your talent acquisition process lives in someone's head or a shared spreadsheet, that is the real risk to your next phase of growth.

Read the full article here and ask yourself whether your hiring infrastructure is built to scale: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMinwFBVV95cUxOYjVkTXhZazZ5NG5PbGVJUTd0RkI5STBHb1Vuc3RJT3VSeVFiTjk3Qm9MU3Nhb3Vwa1pXSXR4SXVHWjhuMUhSTkY3RkVTOFNVV1NpYVZPNGZQNGY4YlJ4Q095VHpBMlZ1bEZacWdOMEItYzRlT0NZaDIwMVhwNHYzLVJybVRTbHRVYlIybGc3OWRVQ09QdFJ0dlVFZ1plaE0

post3.text:
WorkWave just named a new Chief Human Resources Officer. That is a signal, not just a hire.

When a growing company elevates a people leader at that level, it usually means one of two things: they are ahead of the curve, or they are already behind it and know it.

Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business, titled The Talent Engine, tackles this exact inflection point. Authors Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West lay out what it actually takes to build a talent function that drives growth rather than just supports it.

One thing they make clear: the companies that scale well do not treat people strategy as an HR problem. They treat it as a business model decision.

There is a framework in this chapter that will change how you think about your next leadership hire.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not mean better decisions. For most companies between $50M and $500M, they mean slower ones.

Hootsuite recently published a list of 31 social media metrics worth tracking in 2026. Thirty-one. For one channel. That number tells you everything about where business measurement culture is headed, and not in a good direction.

Here is what we see consistently in scaling companies:

First, when everyone is accountable for a dozen metrics, no one is truly accountable for any of them. Ownership dissolves into noise.

Second, the metrics leaders obsess over are often lag indicators. They measure what already happened, not what is about to go wrong.

Third, the most dangerous KPI is the one that looks healthy while the business quietly erodes underneath it. Revenue can rise while margins collapse. Headcount can grow while productivity shrinks.

The discipline is not in tracking more. It is in tracking fewer things that actually drive the outcomes you care about.

What is the one metric your leadership team would fight to keep if you had to cut everything else?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite breaks down 30 financial metrics and KPIs businesses should track heading into 2026. It is a solid reference, and the list is thorough.

But here is the problem we see with scaling companies: a comprehensive list is not a strategy.

When you are moving from $50M toward $500M, the volume of available data explodes. Finance teams can measure almost anything. The leaders who scale well are not the ones measuring the most. They are the ones who have made hard choices about which three to five numbers actually reflect the health and trajectory of the business.

If your leadership team cannot recite your critical numbers from memory, you have too many.

Read the NetSuite piece as a menu, not a checklist: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikwFBVV95cUxNcThuZllxNkVka0dpOV9QdHZQM2RiU0tfMGVIR05tdW9ZN1AtYngwQ1d4WDFSb3ZNSUxKNHFCSUR4aC1lR1g2ZWYzWFE0NWF1WmVpejAxOW9VRFdJa01yLUFKa1hvbjNGQnR6a2hZcVVtQzgwRXNCdXVGbjhfNWR2eWpTSlFyRk5zLVZ3MnJvMU14ZjA

post3.text:
Business.com recently rounded up 14 tools for tracking KPIs. The tools are fine. The problem usually is not the tooling.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business, titled Death by KPIs, goes straight at this. Written by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, the chapter addresses something most scaling companies do not want to admit: the act of measuring can become a substitute for leading.

One insight the authors surface is that as companies grow, KPI lists tend to grow with them, not because the business needs more measurement, but because more measurement feels like control. It is not. It is noise dressed up as rigor.

If your team spends more time updating dashboards than acting on what they show, Chapter 7 was written for you.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most leadership teams think their KPI problem is a tracking problem. It is not. It is a prioritization problem. When every department has fifteen metrics and every meeting reviews all of them, nothing actually gets managed. For companies scaling past $50M, the measurement conversation needs to change from how do we track more to what are we willing to stop measuring.

post1.text:
AI is making your team more productive and that might be the most dangerous thing happening in your business right now.

Here is the problem: productivity gains are visible. ROI is not. A recent report found that UK CEOs widely acknowledge AI is helping their teams get more done, but most cannot connect that output to revenue, margin, or growth. That gap is not a technology problem. It is a strategy problem.

For leaders scaling through the $50M to $500M range, three things matter more than any AI tool you buy:

1. Define what productivity is supposed to produce. Faster work that drives no revenue is just faster waste.

2. Audit before you automate. AI amplifies your existing processes, good and bad.

3. Measure twice, implement once. Set a ROI baseline before the rollout, not six months after.

The companies winning with AI are not the ones moving fastest. They are the ones moving with intention.

What does AI actually need to deliver in your business to justify the investment?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Okoone raised a warning that more scaling companies need to hear: using AI as a reason to cut headcount may create a far more expensive problem down the road.

The core finding is straightforward. Companies that reduce staff based on AI productivity assumptions are discovering those assumptions were wrong, and rehiring is costing them significantly more than the savings they captured.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern with companies in the $50M to $500M range all the time. The pressure to show efficiency gains leads to structural decisions that are very hard to reverse. Talent, institutional knowledge, and culture do not wait for you to course-correct.

Before you let AI justify a workforce reduction, make sure the productivity gains are proven, sustained, and fully understood. Read the full piece here and think carefully about what it means for your next planning cycle.

post3.text:
Newsweek recently asked a question that every growth-stage company should be sitting with: AI is boosting productivity, but is it actually worth it?

Chapter 8 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, takes that question seriously. The chapter is called The Third Monitor Theory, written by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, and it offers a framework for how leaders at scaling companies should think about AI adoption before they commit resources, restructure teams, or overhaul operations.

The core idea is not about whether AI is powerful. It clearly is. The real question is whether your business is positioned to capture that power in a way that compounds over time rather than creates new costs and confusion.

One insight from the chapter: the way you introduce AI inside your organization matters as much as the tools you choose. Most leaders get that backwards.

Rock Your Business is available soon. Follow us for updates.

They are adopting it smarter, with clearer intent, better baselines, and leadership teams that know how to separate genuine ROI from the appearance of progress.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to destroy their companies are the ones who stopped doubting themselves.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a weakness to overcome. It is not. For leaders scaling past $50M, it is often the last honest signal they are getting about where they actually stand.

Forbes Australia recently reported that imposter syndrome tends to follow high achievers straight to the top, not because they are underqualified, but because the stakes keep rising faster than their confidence can settle. That pattern is not a flaw in the leader. It is a feature of the environment.

Here is what that means practically:

First, the doubt you feel about a new market or a new hire is your pattern recognition working. Do not silence it. Interrogate it.

Second, leaders who perform certainty to their teams end up with teams that stop surfacing problems. That is the real risk.

Third, the goal is not confidence. The goal is clarity. Those are very different things.

So the question worth sitting with: Is your leadership team confusing composure with competence?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Campaign US makes a case that is worth paying attention to: stop trying to eliminate imposter syndrome and start putting it to work.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this reframe is not just useful, it is urgent. At that growth stage, leaders are constantly operating in territory they have never been in before. The self-doubt that shows up is not a sign someone is wrong for the role. It is a sign they are taking the role seriously.

The real danger is not leaders who feel the pressure. It is leaders who have learned to perform confidence so well they stop listening to the doubt that could actually protect the business.

If your leadership team is scaling fast, the question is not how to feel more confident. It is how to build a culture where honest uncertainty is treated as information, not weakness.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikgFBVV95cUxNS0JPUmJPTk9IMzNvR21BSC03djE4MDZhVko0eFNpaDZnUzl4MnpTUTBfVFJacUZrNm8tNm5KYXdIUmtwR0FVN0trR2lwcHVFQ3ZIZlJORUJZcUo3VUtnOGhycm1pcmY3WGh5ckQxU1NrU1cyc01PbllsblhxSTAzUzA0bkRheUthNkhhSXl5Sjd1dw?oc=5

post3.text:
There is a question sitting inside Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business that stops a lot of leaders cold: How could you be successful and not have it?

The "it" is imposter syndrome. And the point is not to be provocative. It is to reframe what self-doubt actually signals at the leadership level.

Chapter 9, written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, goes beyond the usual conversation about confidence and psychology. It examines why the leaders who are growing fastest are often the ones carrying the most doubt, and what separates the ones who use it from the ones who unravel under it.

One insight worth previewing: the way a leader relates to their own uncertainty has a direct effect on how safe their team feels telling the truth.

That connection has real operational consequences for any company scaling toward $500M.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Every leader scaling past $50M knows the feeling: you have the results, the title, and the track record, and yet something keeps whispering that the next mistake will expose you. Most leadership advice tells you to push past that feeling. The research, and the leaders who have actually made it to $500M, suggest a very different approach.

post1.text:
The most dangerous thing a $50M+ CEO can do is optimize their business while ignoring their life.

Most leaders at this scale have built financial sophistication into their companies but have done almost no structured thinking about what they actually want their life to look like. Deutsche Bank's wealth planning research for founders makes this point clearly: wealth accumulation without a personal life framework often produces regret, not freedom.

Here is what that costs you in practice:

1. You make exit or reinvestment decisions based on business logic alone, not on what you genuinely want next.

2. Your team can sense when you are running on fumes and obligation rather than intention. It affects culture.

3. The skills that scaled your company, speed, pressure, relentless focus, are actively harmful to the personal clarity work that life planning requires.

Life planning is not a soft skill. At this stage, it is a strategic one. The leaders who scale well are the ones who decide what they are scaling toward.

What does the next chapter of your life actually look like, and have you written it down?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Deutsche Bank Wealth Management on financial planning for entrepreneurs and founders surfaces something scaling companies rarely address directly: founders often accumulate significant wealth while remaining completely unclear on what that wealth is supposed to do for their lives.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly in companies moving from $50M toward $500M. The business demands intensify, the personal planning stalls, and leaders arrive at major inflection points without a clear personal framework to guide the decisions in front of them.

Wealth without a life plan is just a bigger number.

If you are leading a company at this stage, the financial and personal conversations need to happen in parallel, not sequentially. Your next growth phase will demand more of you, not less.

Read the full piece and start asking the harder questions: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxQOTFRM1pIdEtXSndlcGN4blIxdlc3RHVLVmRuTkRGTFlzTU91X1YzZzNfTk9YNmtHS3psaHlFX3I1V3JWR2NYYzFpQ1NPazIzWFVHaTlRNHFFUFVLTHJJQkZMV1RwX3BOaWhzNTZjRmlMUXBhMHhuNHdKUFJOSEtINko4YnpWQ0FWYWozY0Iza2JJVzh3NGg2UjYtM0F4RDRZR25zbXN0Ykd6TG9qOV9FcA?oc=5

post3.text:
Wealth planning for founders gets a lot of attention. Life planning for founders almost never does. Those are not the same thing.

Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled Coming Up for Air. Authored by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, this chapter addresses what most scaling frameworks leave out entirely: the intentional design of your life alongside the growth of your business.

One of the core ideas in the chapter is that leaders scaling toward $500M are often so deep inside the machine they have lost the ability to ask the most important question of this stage: what is this all actually for?

Samantha, Jonathan, and Katherine do not offer a productivity hack. They offer a framework for the harder conversation that high-growth leaders consistently avoid.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Every system in your company has a plan. Your supply chain, your sales pipeline, your hiring roadmap. But what about your life? Leaders scaling from $50M to $500M are making decisions daily that will define the next decade, often with no personal framework to guide them. Here is why life planning is the missing strategic layer in most growth strategies.
